content: Nocturnal asthma is characterized by a reduction in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) of at least 15% between the time of going to bed and waking up in individuals who have both clinical and physiological evidence of asthma. The underlying mechanisms of nocturnal asthma are strongly linked to chronobiology, which is the study of biological processes that follow time-related rhythms. Therefore, understanding the circadian rhythm is crucial for interpreting the changes in lung function that occur in asthmatic patients during sleep. A large population-based study found that episodes of shortness of breath in asthmatic individuals, when untreated, most frequently occurred between 10:00 PM and 7:00 AM. Another survey, which included 7,729 patients, revealed that approximately 74% of individuals with asthma woke up at least once a week due to symptoms, 64% woke up three times per week, and 39% experienced nightly awakenings caused by asthma symptoms. The nocturnal worsening of asthma is a very common clinical phenomenon. It affects about 75% of individuals with asthma, who report waking up at least once per week due to symptoms. Furthermore, approximately 40% of asthmatic patients experience nocturnal symptoms every night.
